# Disagreement Log — T12_012 (Testament of Benjamin)
**Chapter:** T12_012 | **Verses:** 10 sections (~12 verses)
**Translators compared:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA | **Arbiter:** SOPHIA

| # | Verse | Issue | EMET | LOGOS | PNEUMA | SOPHIA ruling |
|---|-------|-------|------|-------|--------|---------------|
| 1 | 1:6 | Name etymology | "Benjamin, that-is, a-son-of-days" | Not present | Not present | EMET preserves the etymology explanation; SOPHIA includes as it reflects the Greek MS annotation |
| 2 | 4:3 | Jacob's prophecy over Joseph | "Lamb-of-God...blood-of-the-covenant...destroy-Beliar" | Same | Narrative paraphrase in context | EMET/LOGOS exact wording adopted — this is among the most theologically loaded sentences in the corpus |
| 3 | 7:5–9 | Resurrection sequence | Full sequence: Enoch, Noah, Shem etc. | Same | Full sequence presented narratively | All three agree on content; SOPHIA preserves the specific patriarch list exactly |
| 4 | 7:9 | "God in the flesh" | "appeared-as-God-in-the-flesh-to-deliver-them" | "appeared as God in the flesh to deliver them" | "appeared as God in the flesh to rescue them" | All three agree — this phrase (en sarki epiphanenta) is the most explicit incarnation statement in the Testaments |
| 5 | 9:3 | "Strain of music" | "strain-of-music-in-the-mouth-of-all" | "strain of music in the mouth of all" | "like a song on everyone's lips" | "strain of music in the mouth of all" — EMET/LOGOS; PNEUMA's paraphrase loses the Greek melos (melody/strain) |

---
*SOPHIA notes: Testament of Benjamin is the eschatological capstone of the entire Testaments collection. The resurrection vision (7:5–9) is the most detailed and explicit in the corpus, culminating in the remarkable phrase "appeared as God in the flesh" — an unambiguous incarnation claim. Jacob's prophecy over Joseph (4:3) also contains "blood of the covenant" — a eucharistic formula. These passages are almost certainly Christian insertions into an originally Jewish document, but SOPHIA retains them without emendation as they appear in Codex Cantabrigiensis. The "ravening wolf" reference (9:1) inverts Jacob's blessing over Benjamin in Genesis 49:27 — he who was the wolf becomes the distributor of bread. Benjamin's death — falling into "a sweet sleep" and found dead in the morning — is the most peaceful death scene in the Testaments.*
